item.title: Hackers Heat Supermarket Fridges to 50°C in France Cyberattack
item.description:
Hackers reportedly heated supermarket fridges to 50°C in France, spoiling food stocks, while stores in the Netherlands and Belgium faced separate IT outages.

Supermarkets in France are dealing with large food losses after a cyberattack reportedly targeted refrigeration-control systems and forced equipment to heat instead of keeping products cold.

According to French reporting citing BFMTV, the attack began overnight from Sunday to Monday and affected refrigeration systems linked to Danish manufacturer Danfoss. The unknown attackers reportedly abused the defrosting function in older control software, setting some equipment to heat continuously, with temperatures said to have reached 50°C.

The cyber attack impacted several major supermarket chains, including Intermarché, Super U and E.Leclerc. Metro stores and smaller independent businesses, including butcher shops, were also reported to have been hit.

French outlets including Clubic, 01net and Capital reported that around 150 Intermarché stores may have been affected. The total number of affected locations has not yet been confirmed.

Stores Forced to Throw Away Food

The impact was visible quickly because the cyberattack hit systems used to preserve fresh and frozen products. Once the cold chain was broken, stores had to discard goods rather than risk selling unsafe food.

In Haguenau, Alsace, an Intermarché store reportedly lost its frozen-food stock, worth about €50,000. A nearby Super U reportedly discarded both fresh and frozen products, with losses estimated at about €220,000. An E.Leclerc store in the same town was also affected, although its losses had not been calculated at the time of reporting.

The confirmed losses from the two Haguenau stores alone were reported at about €270,000. If the number of affected stores is confirmed, the total damage could reach several million euros.

Coopérative U acknowledged that refrigeration installations in several stores had been affected and said teams were working with refrigeration specialists to restore service. Intermarché also reportedly warned internally that several stores had lost frozen products.

Danfoss Systems Named in Reports

The reported target was not supermarket payment systems, customer accounts or e-commerce sites, but equipment used to control refrigeration.

Refrigeration-control software can manage cooling, temperature settings and defrost cycles. A defrost cycle is normally a controlled process used to prevent ice buildup, but the reports say attackers manipulated that function so equipment heated for far longer than intended.

Danfoss has been named in French reporting as the supplier of the affected refrigeration-control systems. At the time of writing, the reports reviewed by Hackread.com did not include a public statement from Danfoss confirming the technical cause or naming the affected software versions.

The identity of the attackers has also not been confirmed. It is also unclear whether the attack involved exposed remote access, compromised credentials, unpatched vulnerabilities, or another route into the control systems.

Dutch Retailer Reports Separate Cybersecurity Incident

A separate retail disruption is also affecting Ahold Delhaize brands in the Netherlands and Belgium, although no public evidence currently links it to the French refrigeration attack.

Dutch public broadcaster NOS reported that Albert Heijn, Etos and Gall & Gall have suffered disruption since Sunday afternoon after what parent company Ahold Delhaize described as a “cybersecurity incident.” Albert Heijn had earlier referred to it as an IT incident.

The disruption was not limited to store systems. Albert Heijn’s websites, apps and customer service were unavailable, online grocery deliveries were paused, loyalty systems stopped working and some electronic shelf labels still showed last week’s promotional prices. Delhaize in Belgium also reported problems, with customers unable to place new online orders or reach customer service.

Ahold Delhaize said it had taken immediate measures to protect its IT environment, including temporarily switching off some systems as a precaution. The company said it was investigating the incident and working to restore services, with protection of customer, employee and partner data as a priority.

For now, the French refrigeration attack and the Ahold Delhaize disruption should be treated as separate incidents unless investigators or the companies say otherwise.

I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: Why Robust VPS Hosting Helps OpenClaw Run Faster and More Reliably
item.description:
OpenClaw is not a chatbot that waits for a prompt. It is an autonomous agent that runs real computer tasks, remembers what it has done, and stays connected to the messaging apps you already use, all day and all night.

That kind of nonstop work asks a lot of the machine underneath it. Run it on a shared box or a home computer and the cracks can show fast. Put it on a strong virtual private server, and the experience becomes faster, steadier, and easier to rely on.

The reason is simple: an agent that never sleeps needs resources that are always available. Here is how robust hosting removes the limits that can hold OpenClaw back.

Why an Autonomous Agent Is So Demanding

Before looking at hardware, it helps to understand what the agent is doing behind the scenes, because that workload is heavier than it first appears.

It Runs Nonstop, Not on Request

A normal app answers a request and goes quiet. OpenClaw works differently. It keeps a process running around the clock, holding on to context, user preferences, and project states so nothing resets between sessions. At the same time, it can juggle scheduled jobs, read files, and run commands in the background.

All of that needs memory and processing power that stay available, not resources that disappear when another user on a shared server gets busy. When those resources drop at the wrong moment, a scheduled job can fail, a task can slow down, or the agent can fall behind on work you expected it to handle.

It Works Beyond the Chat Window

The agent does more than send messages. It can open web pages, work through them, extract the data you asked for, and act on what it finds. On a personal laptop, that browser activity competes with everything else running on the machine and can quickly slow things down.

On a dedicated server, the same work happens separately from your day-to-day device. That means OpenClaw can keep working in the background without dragging down your laptop or interrupting other tasks. With fewer local limits, jobs finish faster and results are more consistent.

Hardware That Clears the Bottlenecks

Once you understand that the agent runs hard and never stops, the value of stronger hardware becomes clear. Each part of the server removes a different drag on performance.

Fast Storage and Enough Memory

Speed starts with storage. Fast solid-state drives help the agent retrieve saved context, files, and database lookups quickly, so tasks do not stall midway. Memory matters just as much. A robust VPS gives OpenClaw enough RAM to run several workflows at once and handle larger workloads without choking.

That extra headroom also matters as you add skills, integrations, and background jobs. Each one draws from the same pool of memory. If the server is already stretched, performance drops. If there is room to work, the agent stays responsive even when the workload grows.

Dedicated Processing Power

Shared hosting splits processor time and memory across many users. That means your agent can slow down whenever another account on the same machine starts using more resources. For an always-on autonomous agent, that inconsistency creates problems.

Using VPS hosting for OpenClaw gives the agent more consistent compute resources, so heavier scripts, browser tasks, and multi-step reasoning can run more steadily. The exact performance gain depends on the workload, server configuration, and how OpenClaw is set up, but dedicated resources give the system a much stronger foundation.

Stable Network and Uptime

Strong hardware only helps if the agent can be reached and can reach external services reliably. That is where the network side matters.

Awake and Responsive Around the Clock

A home or office connection was never built to host an always-on agent. Devices sleep, IP addresses can change, and bandwidth can run thin when other activity picks up. A server in a professional data center stays online even when your own devices are turned off.

Hosting closer to users can also reduce response times for webhooks and API calls. Better bandwidth helps with steady web work, file transfers, and background tasks, so the agent does not get stuck waiting on a weak connection. The result is simple: OpenClaw is more likely to respond when it is needed, instead of waiting for the network to recover.

Built to Keep Running

Consistent uptime becomes important when a business starts depending on the agent. If the server behind it keeps running, the work it supports keeps moving with fewer gaps. That reliability also makes it easier to plan for backups, recovery, monitoring, and other steps that keep operations steady if something goes wrong.

Robust hosting does not remove the need for proper configuration, security, and maintenance, but it gives OpenClaw a more dependable base to run from.

Conclusion

Robust VPS hosting does not just keep OpenClaw online. It helps the agent perform the way it was designed to. Fast storage, enough memory, dedicated compute, and a stable network each improve a different part of the workload. Together, they can turn a slow or unreliable setup into one that responds faster and runs more consistently.

For anyone relying on an autonomous agent to handle real work, the server underneath is not a minor detail. It is one of the main factors that decides how well everything else runs.

item.title: G2A.COM Reports 35% Growth in Security Software Orders, Outpacing VPN Growth
item.description:
Amsterdam, Netherlands, October 13th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Antivirus and security software orders grow more than twice as fast as VPN orders, accounting for 43% of cybersecurity purchases on the marketplace 

G2A.COM, a digital marketplace that serves more than 35 million users across 180 countries, reports a 35% year-on-year surge in antivirus and security software orders, outpacing VPN orders.   

Released during Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the marketplace figures reveal that security software accounted for 43% of cybersecurity-related orders during the period, up from 39% in the equivalent period in 2025. Overall, orders across cybersecurity products increased by almost a quarter (24%).  

VPNs remain the larger category, but antivirus and security software are taking a greater share of purchases on G2A.COM. The findings highlight that consumers are increasingly looking beyond privacy and secure connectivity towards broader protection of their devices, accounts and digital activity 

The trend comes as the global cyber threat landscape continues to evolve. According to the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) Threat Landscape 2026, ransomware remains the most impactful type of cyber incident in the short term, while social engineering continues to be widely used to exploit trust.  

“What we’re seeing is a shift from privacy-first protection towards a more layered approach to cybersecurity” said Adrian Podkaminer, Chief Information Security Officer at G2A.COM. “As people move between more devices, accounts and digital services, effective cybersecurity increasingly depends on different safeguards working together rather than relying on a single solution.” 

G2A.COM marketplace data suggests that consumers are taking a more active approach to protecting their digital lives. At the same time, they do not see security as their responsibility alone. According to the Trust in Digital Commerce report, a survey by G2A.COM and Juniper Research involving 9,000 consumers from nine countries found that half of them think e-commerce sites are mainly responsible for security. Meanwhile, a third blame banks and payment providers, and 20% say it’s up to the consumers themselves. 

For G2A.COM, that responsibility translates into concrete safeguards. The marketplace works exclusively with verified business sellers and applies KYC, KYB and AML processes, supported by AI-based fraud prevention and continuous monitoring. 

Cybersecurity Awareness Month offers an opportunity for consumers to review both the tools they use and the habits that help protect their accounts. G2A.COM encourages users to: 

  • Secure important accounts: use strong, unique passwords and enable multi-factor authentication wherever available, particularly for email, shopping and payment accounts. 
  • Keep devices updated: install operating system, browser and application updates promptly. 
  • Check before clicking: treat unexpected login requests, downloads and urgent payment messages cautiously, and visit the official website or app directly. 
  • Understand the protection purchased: check what a security product covers, its compatibility with existing devices and any subscription or renewal terms. 

About G2A.COM 

G2A.COM is the world’s largest marketplace for digital entertainment, serving over 35 million users from 180 countries with more than 200 million visits in 2025. As a true gateway to digital entertainment and a rapidly evolving digital ecosystem, G2A.COM gives access to over 125,000 digital offerings, including vouchers, games, DLCs, in-game items, and non-gaming items such as gift cards, subscriptions, software, or e-learning, sold by sellers from all over the world. A compliance-driven organization audited by Deloitte for over a decade, G2A.COM is a leader in online security, recognized by the prestigious American CNP Award alongside industry giants like Microsoft and PayPal. Today, the company is a key gateway for recognized global brands, leveraging its scalable infrastructure to drive the next phase of e-commerce through agentic AI and global M&A – continuously expanding its role as the Gate 2 Adventure in the digital world.

item.title: Amazon Fire TV Cube Rooted Using Four-Year-Old Arm Mali Vulnerability
item.description:
A four-year-old Arm Mali GPU vulnerability can be used to root the third-generation Amazon Fire TV Cube, but its patch status remains unclear.

A vulnerability in Arm’s Mali GPU driver, first disclosed four years ago, has been adapted to gain root access to the third-generation Amazon Fire TV Cube, allowing users to remove Amazon’s software restrictions and install alternative operating systems, according to Cybernews research shared with Hackread.com.

The exploit uses CVE-2022-38181 (CVSS 8.8), a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in the Arm Mali GPU kernel driver. The bug involves memory that the driver frees while it may still be in use, creating an opportunity to manipulate kernel memory and gain elevated privileges.

Security researcher Man Yue Mo reported the vulnerability to the Android security team on July 12, 2022. His original proof of concept showed how an unprivileged Android process could exploit the bug to execute code in the kernel and gain root access on a Google Pixel 6.

What the Fire TV Cube Exploit Allows

Mo’s technical write-up explains that the process can trigger memory pressure through standard system calls, prompting the driver to free active Just-In-Time (JIT) memory allocations. By manipulating how the kernel reuses that memory, the process can overwrite internal driver structures and take control of kernel space, ultimately gaining root privileges.

Arm released a fix in Mali driver version r40p0 on October 7, 2022. The third-generation Fire TV Cube launched on October 25 that year, but it remains unclear whether Amazon incorporated the fix into FireOS or whether the vulnerable driver remained present on the device.

What Root Access Lets Users Do

Later, a developer using the alias Pro-me3us shared an adapted version of the exploit on XDA Forums, making it work with FireOS’s 32-bit userspace. With root access, users can install Magisk, replace the Fire TV Cube’s stock recovery system, and load other operating systems.

These include CoreELEC, a Linux-based system built around Kodi for media playback, and EmuELEC, which focuses on retro gaming. Both give users alternatives to Amazon’s standard software, particularly those who want to play local media files or run games on the device.

“For casual Netflix viewers, this might not mean much, but it’s very important for home theater enthusiasts with multi-channel audio setups and the itch to see the content at maximum quality, as the creators intended,” Cybernews noted.

Amazon Says Physical Access Is Required

Amazon told Cybernews that the demonstrated method poses little risk to customers because it requires physical access and deliberate, multiple-step modifications.

“Protecting the security of our customers and devices is our top priority,” an Amazon spokesperson said. “What’s being demonstrated poses little risk to customers; it’s someone modifying a device they own to run unofficial software, which requires direct physical access and a deliberate, multi-step process.”

Since the exploit requires code to run on the device first, the vulnerability alone does not put every Fire TV Cube owner at immediate risk. However, root access could expose data or allow further malicious activity if abused. Cybernews reported no evidence that the exploit was being used in real-world attacks.

Amazon has yet to confirm whether CVE-2022-38181 has been patched in the Fire TV Cube. Until the device’s patch status is clarified, users should be cautious about modifying the system or installing unofficial software.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Powering Proactive Defense: How MSSPs Can Strengthen Threat Hunting Against Ransomware
item.description:
Ransomware defense cannot rely on alerts alone. For MSSPs in particular, the ability to proactively hunt for attacker infrastructure and emerging campaigns can mean finding threats before they become major incidents.

Threat intelligence feeds give security teams a way to make threat hunting more continuous and scalable. By feeding fresh, actionable intelligence into the solutions analysts already use, they can turn external threat activity into concrete hunting opportunities across customer environments.

The Role of Threat Hunting in Modern MSSP Security

Threat hunting gives MSSPs a proactive way to identify suspicious activity that may not trigger existing detections.

Customers expect their security provider to identify threats before they result in disruption, data loss, or costly incident response. That means an MSSP team needs to do more than respond to alerts generated by individual customer environments. It has to understand what attackers are doing outside those environments and use that intelligence to look for relevant activity inside them.

item.description:
Torrance, California, October 13th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Criminal IP, developed by AI SPERA, will participate in Security Days Fall 2026 Tokyo, taking place October 21–23, 2026, at the TAKANAWA GATEWAY Convention Center. At booth B20, Criminal IP will showcase Criminal IP Threat Intelligence (Criminal IP TI) and Criminal IP AITEM (AI-Powered Threat Exposure Management) through live demonstrations focused on threat investigation and exposure management.

As cloud adoption and connections with business partners expand, organizations need to understand risks beyond their internally managed assets. Internet-exposed services, vulnerabilities, attacker infrastructure, and leaked information all contribute to a broader attack surface. Criminal IP will demonstrate how security teams can connect these findings to support investigation and prioritize response.

Explore Practical Security Workflows at Booth B20

Visitors can see how Criminal IP supports everyday security tasks, from investigating suspicious indicators to identifying assets and risks that require attention. Demonstrations will cover:

  • Investigating threat information associated with IP addresses, domains, and URLs.
  • Analyzing malicious infrastructure, vulnerabilities, and threat actor information.
  • Discovering internet-exposed IT assets and services.
  • Using AI-assisted analysis to investigate and prioritize exposure risks.
  • Identifying leaked information on the dark web.
  • Assessing risks involving business partners and affiliated companies.

item.title: SerpApi Expands Beyond Search Results with New Extract API
item.description:
AUSTIN, TX – October 13, 2026 – SerpApi today announced the launch of Extract API, a new capability that helps developers retrieve real-time data from publicly available web pages in easy-to-use formats. The release expands SerpApi beyond search result retrieval, helping developers move from discovering relevant web pages to accessing the structured content behind them. With Extract API, developers can search, discover, and extract public web data within a single workflow.

For developers building AI applications, research platforms, and data-driven products, finding a relevant URL is often only the first step. Turning web pages into usable data frequently requires custom scrapers, parsing logic, and website-specific extraction workflows that add complexity and maintenance overhead.

With Extract API, developers can start with a single URL, discover additional pages across a website, and extract structured content in formats suitable for downstream applications and AI workflows. While developers often rely on separate tools for search, extraction, and crawling, Extract API brings these capabilities together within the existing SerpApi platform, API ecosystem, and developer workflow.

“For years, we’ve helped developers find information on the web through search engine result page APIs,” said Julien Khaleghy, CEO and founder of SerpApi.

“But finding a page is often just the first step. Developers increasingly need access to the content behind those results for AI agents, research workflows, and data-driven applications. With Extract API, we’re making it easier to extract structured content from public web pages without the burden of building and maintaining extraction infrastructure,” Julien explained.

As organizations build AI applications, research tools, monitoring systems, and data-driven products, the need for reliable access to web-based information continues to grow. Developers increasingly need more than URLs, requiring structured content, metadata, links, and other signals that can be consumed by applications and AI workflows.

Extract API addresses these needs by transforming supported public web pages into normalized, structured data that can be consumed by applications, knowledge systems, and AI tools.

Potential use cases include:

  • AI agents that need access to webpage content and supporting evidence
  • Research platforms that collect information from public websites
  • Product and market monitoring workflows
  • SEO and content discovery initiatives
  • Internal knowledge enrichment and retrieval systems

Extract API is now available across all SerpApi accounts and supports extraction of publicly available web pages through a generic extraction workflow.

Because extraction relies on a generalized parser, website support may vary. Some URLs covered by dedicated SerpApi engines may return the schema associated with that specialized engine. Crawl usage is billed based on successfully extracted pages.

For more information about Extract API, visit serpapi.com/blog/introducing-extract-api/

About SerpApi

SerpApi is the world’s leading provider of search data, pioneering APIs that turn search engine results into structured, developer-ready information. Founded in 2017, the company enables developers, researchers, Fortune 500 companies, and organizations around the world to integrate live search insights from sources like Google, Bing, and YouTube into applications, analytics, and research workflows.

With more than 100 specialized APIs, SerpApi supports use cases ranging from AI development and machine learning to SEO monitoring, cybersecurity intelligence, and e-commerce analysis, helping teams build reliable, data-driven products at scale.

item.title: MS Teams Phishing, ClickFix and Shai-Hulud npm Attacks Dominate Threat Report
item.description:
Ontinue’s 1H 2026 threat report shows attackers increasingly abusing Microsoft Teams, npm packages, device-code logins and blockchain ClickFix tactics to steal access and spread malware.

Cybercriminals are increasingly abusing legitimate business tools to access organizations, steal credentials and spread malware, rather than relying only on software vulnerabilities, according to Ontinue’s 1H 2026 Threat Intelligence Report.

The report describes how these tactics are showing up across workplace communications, Microsoft authentication and software supply chains.

Fake IT Support on Microsoft Teams

Ontinue found that attackers continued impersonating IT support staff through Microsoft Teams during the first half of 2026. The approach involves contacting employees from outside their organizations and posing as colleagues or help-desk staff to convince them to take actions that give attackers access.

The company examined 393,433 external contacts across 42,240 outside organizations. About one in every 990 external contacts showed signs of IT-support impersonation. Around 30% of the organizations monitored by Ontinue had at least one such contact, although the figures do not confirm that a compromise occurred.

Black Basta affiliates used the technique in 2024. The group later fragmented after its internal chats leaked in February 2025, but other threat actors continued using similar tactics.

Shai-Hulud and the Software Supply Chain

The report examines Shai-Hulud, an npm worm that targets developer credentials to spread through the software supply chain. The worm runs during package installation, downloads the Bun JavaScript runtime and uses TruffleHog to search for exposed secrets.

It can then use stolen npm tokens to publish compromised packages, while malicious GitHub workflows and self-hosted runners help it continue spreading. The worm also publishes stolen credentials to public GitHub repositories, exposing them to further abuse.

Hackread.com previously reported a Shai-Hulud resurgence affecting more than 1,280 npm packages, including packages used across widely downloaded JavaScript projects.

Ontinue also cites controlled evaluations by the UK AI Security Institute in which AI agents exceeded their assigned testing scope. One agent submitted a malicious pull request and created fake GitHub accounts to promote it. The findings raise questions about how autonomous agents could be abused, but do not establish a successful real-world supply-chain breach.

Microsoft Authentication Under Attack

Between May and June 2026, Ontinue confirmed ten device-code phishing compromises across five customer tenants. The affected sectors were professional services, industrial automation, industrial equipment manufacturing, financial services and research.

In these attacks, victims entered authentication codes into Microsoft’s legitimate sign-in flow, allowing attackers to obtain refresh tokens. Researchers observed operators replaying tokens, obtaining Primary Refresh Token material and registering unauthorized devices to maintain access. Some cases had no corresponding default Microsoft Sentinel alert when discovered.

ClickFix Moves to Blockchain

Ontinue’s ten-week ClickFix analysis recorded 10,818 scans, of which 6,276, or 58%, were classified as malicious. Researchers identified 6,188 delivery domains linked to just 158 payload hosts, showing how a large pool of domains can funnel victims toward a much smaller set of malware servers.

The report also found that 1,568 malicious findings, or 25.3%, used EtherHiding to retrieve payloads through blockchain infrastructure. Six distinct smart-contract addresses were identified.

Experts’ Commentary

The findings highlight how attackers exploit trusted communication channels and authentication processes rather than relying solely on technical vulnerabilities. Several cybersecurity experts shared comments with Hackread.com, emphasizing that organizations need stronger identity verification and consistent monitoring of trusted systems.

Jason Soroko, Senior Fellow at Sectigo, said attackers exploit both trust in IT support workflows and the lack of cryptographic verification during human interactions.

“Help desks exist to assist employees facing access issues and typically rely on fragile knowledge-based authentication that skilled threat actors bypass effortlessly,” Soroko said. He called for stronger identity verification, including “mandatory video verification and certificate based authentication.”

Shane Barney, Chief Information Security Officer at Keeper Security, said attackers increasingly target systems organizations already trust rather than looking for weaknesses in traditional network perimeters.

“Collaboration platforms, identity providers, and third-party integrations all carry implicit trust that rarely gets the same scrutiny as administrative access or privileged accounts. That is the blind spot,” Barney said. He urged organizations to apply zero-trust principles consistently, validating every session, monitoring access paths and flagging unusual behavior, even when activity comes through trusted tools.

Kern Smith, Vice President of Global Solutions at Zimperium, warned that phishing campaigns have evolved to target authentication processes, particularly on mobile devices.

“Phishing has evolved into real-time, interactive deception designed to defeat MFA, especially on mobile devices,” Smith said. He added that defenses should combine strong identity platforms with on-device mobile threat detection to prevent credentials and sessions from being exposed.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

The report examines Shai-Hulud, an npm worm that targets developer credentials to spread through the software supply chain. The worm runs during package installation, downloads the Bun JavaScript runtime and uses TruffleHog to search for exposed secrets.

It can then use stolen npm tokens to publish compromised packages, while malicious GitHub workflows and self-hosted runners help it continue spreading. The worm also publishes stolen credentials to public GitHub repositories, exposing them to further abuse.

Hackread.com previously reported a Shai-Hulud resurgence affecting more than 1,280 npm packages, including packages used across widely downloaded JavaScript projects.

Ontinue also cites controlled evaluations by the UK AI Security Institute in which AI agents exceeded their assigned testing scope. One agent submitted a malicious pull request and created fake GitHub accounts to promote it. The findings raise questions about how autonomous agents could be abused, but do not establish a successful real-world supply-chain breach.

Microsoft Authentication Under Attack

Between May and June 2026, Ontinue confirmed ten device-code phishing compromises across five customer tenants. The affected sectors were professional services, industrial automation, industrial equipment manufacturing, financial services and research.

In these attacks, victims entered authentication codes into Microsoft’s legitimate sign-in flow, allowing attackers to obtain refresh tokens. Researchers observed operators replaying tokens, obtaining Primary Refresh Token material and registering unauthorized devices to maintain access. Some cases had no corresponding default Microsoft Sentinel alert when discovered.

ClickFix Moves to Blockchain

Ontinue’s ten-week ClickFix analysis recorded 10,818 scans, of which 6,276, or 58%, were classified as malicious. Researchers identified 6,188 delivery domains linked to just 158 payload hosts, showing how a large pool of domains can funnel victims toward a much smaller set of malware servers.

The report also found that 1,568 malicious findings, or 25.3%, used EtherHiding to retrieve payloads through blockchain infrastructure. Six distinct smart-contract addresses were identified.

Experts’ Commentary

The findings highlight how attackers exploit trusted communication channels and authentication processes rather than relying solely on technical vulnerabilities. Several cybersecurity experts shared comments with Hackread.com, emphasizing that organizations need stronger identity verification and consistent monitoring of trusted systems.

Jason Soroko, Senior Fellow at Sectigo, said attackers exploit both trust in IT support workflows and the lack of cryptographic verification during human interactions.

“Help desks exist to assist employees facing access issues and typically rely on fragile knowledge-based authentication that skilled threat actors bypass effortlessly,” Soroko said. He called for stronger identity verification, including “mandatory video verification and certificate based authentication.”

Shane Barney, Chief Information Security Officer at Keeper Security, said attackers increasingly target systems organizations already trust rather than looking for weaknesses in traditional network perimeters.

“Collaboration platforms, identity providers, and third-party integrations all carry implicit trust that rarely gets the same scrutiny as administrative access or privileged accounts. That is the blind spot,” Barney said. He urged organizations to apply zero-trust principles consistently, validating every session, monitoring access paths and flagging unusual behavior, even when activity comes through trusted tools.

Kern Smith, Vice President of Global Solutions at Zimperium, warned that phishing campaigns have evolved to target authentication processes, particularly on mobile devices.

“Phishing has evolved into real-time, interactive deception designed to defeat MFA, especially on mobile devices,” Smith said. He added that defenses should combine strong identity platforms with on-device mobile threat detection to prevent credentials and sessions from being exposed.

item.title: Best NinjaOne Alternatives for Endpoint, Patch, and Vulnerability Management
item.description:
NinjaOne is a broad remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform. Many IT teams, though, spend most of their time on a narrower set of jobs: patching, deploying software, fixing vulnerabilities, and remoting into devices. 

If that sounds like your workload, a focused tool can cover what you need without paying for modules you won’t use. This guide compares five NinjaOne alternatives on scope, OS coverage, vulnerability workflow, and how each one prices.

Key Takeaways

  • Scope: NinjaOne bundles monitoring with options for ticketing, backup, documentation, and mobile device management. Most alternatives here focus on endpoint work.
  • Pricing models differ: The options below use published per-device tiers, per-technician plans, free tiers, or edition-based licensing. NinjaOne sells per endpoint through custom quotes.
  • Vulnerability workflow: The strongest options connect a finding to a fix and a confirmation in one console, so you don’t need a separate scanner.
  • OS coverage: Teams that need Linux should check support carefully, because coverage varies across these tools.

What to Compare Before You Switch

Start with the work your team actually does each week. If most tickets involve outdated software, failed installs, and open CVEs, prioritize deployment and remediation depth over feature count.

Next, check how pricing is built. Some tools publish rates. Others quote per endpoint and price extra modules separately. 

Compare the total cost for your device count, including any tier you’d need for vulnerability management or remote access.

Finally, test offline behavior. Laptops that miss a deployment window should catch up automatically when they reconnect.

The 5 Best NinjaOne Alternatives

1. PDQ Connect

Built for sysadmins who mainly need patching, software deployment, vulnerability remediation, and remote desktop, PDQ offers a cloud endpoint manager for Windows and macOS that works without a VPN. 

Deployments pull from a curated, virus-scanned package library or from custom packages. They can run on a schedule or on triggers, and they queue for offline devices until those devices reconnect.

Best for: Internal IT teams and MSPs managing Windows and macOS fleets that don’t need a full RMM.

Pricing: Published annual tiers of $12 (Basic), $18 (Plus), and $28 (Premium) per device, with a 100-device minimum. The 14-day trial covers up to 250 devices with no credit card.

Where it beats NinjaOne: You get published pricing with no custom quote. Premium adds vulnerability scanning, prioritization, and one-click CVE resolution in the same console.

Trade-off: There’s no Linux support, ticketing, backup, or documentation. The platform integrates with tools like Freshservice, Jira, and Entra ID instead.

2. Atera

Atera combines RMM with a built-in helpdesk. It charges per technician rather than per device, with unlimited endpoints on every plan, and it runs separate plan lines for internal IT departments and MSPs.

Best for: Small teams or MSPs with many devices per technician who want ticketing in the same tool.

Pricing: Per technician per month, with unlimited devices. Extras such as network discovery are sold as add-ons. The 30-day free trial doesn’t need a credit card.

Where it beats NinjaOne: Adding devices doesn’t raise the bill, so growing fleets keep costs predictable.

Trade-off: Anyone who needs console access requires a technician license, so costs rise with team size.

3. Automox

Automox is a cloud-native patching platform for Windows, macOS, and Linux, covering operating system and third-party application updates. Policies run continuously once set, and Worklet scripts extend automation to configuration tasks.

Best for: Teams with Linux endpoints whose main job is keeping systems patched.

Pricing: Per endpoint. The entry tier covers OS patching only, while third-party patching titles sit in custom-priced tiers.

Where it beats NinjaOne: It offers a patch-focused console with Linux coverage and no full RMM to configure.

Trade-off: Third-party application patching requires a quote-based tier, so budget for it up front.

4. Action1

Action1 handles patch management for Windows, macOS, and Linux from a browser, with no VPN required. It covers OS and third-party updates, includes vulnerability assessment, and can patch endpoints while they’re offline.

Best for: Smaller fleets that want to start without a license cost.

Pricing: The first 200 endpoints are free with full functionality. This is a permanent free tier, not a trial. Larger fleets move to a paid plan.

Where it beats NinjaOne: Organizations under 200 endpoints pay nothing for patching and vulnerability visibility.

Trade-off: Native Linux agent support arrived in December 2025, so test it carefully against your distributions.

5. ManageEngine Endpoint Central

Endpoint Central is a unified endpoint management platform covering Windows, Mac, and Linux desktops as well as mobile devices. It’s available as a cloud subscription or an on-premises license.

Best for: Organizations that need on-premises deployment or mobile management in the same tool.

Pricing: A free edition covers up to 25 endpoints. Paid licensing runs across Professional, Enterprise, UEM, and Security editions.

Where it beats NinjaOne: You can run it fully on-premises.

Trade-off: Windows laptop and macOS MDM require the UEM or Security edition, and OS imaging is an add-on in some editions.

When NinjaOne Is Still the Right Call

NinjaOne makes sense when your requirements reach beyond endpoints. It supports Windows, macOS, and Linux, and it offers modules for ticketing, backup, documentation, and mobile device management. 

Each module is priced per endpoint on top of the core subscription, so get a full quote for the modules you’d actually use before comparing totals.

How to Run a Fair Pilot

Use the same representative devices in each tool you shortlist. Push a routine update, force a failed install, and take a laptop offline mid-deployment. Then measure how long it takes to go from a reported vulnerability to a confirmed fix. 

That speed matters most in heavy release months, like when Microsoft’s July 2026 Patch Tuesday shipped fixes for 622 flaws, including two exploited zero-days. Those results will tell you more than any feature checklist.”

FAQ

What’s the cheapest NinjaOne alternative?

Action1 is free for the first 200 endpoints, and ManageEngine Endpoint Central has a free edition for up to 25. For larger fleets, compare published per-device tiers against quoted per-endpoint rates at your actual device count.

Does NinjaOne publish its pricing?

NinjaOne charges per endpoint per month through custom quotes, so confirm rates and module costs with its sales team.

Which alternatives support Linux?

Atera, Automox, Action1, and ManageEngine Endpoint Central support Linux. Check distribution support during your pilot.

Do I need a full RMM?

Only if you need monitoring, ticketing, backup, or documentation in one platform. Teams focused on patching, deployment, and remediation can often use a dedicated endpoint manager instead.

item.title: AI Scams Target Crypto Users, Not Protocols, and Wallet Security Is Catching Up
item.description:
Picture a composite case drawn from documented scams where a tech professional spends forty minutes on a video call with a “compliance officer” whose face and voice were generated by software. 

The scenario is a composite, but each technique in it is real. 

Chainalysis found impersonation scams grew more than 1,400% in 2025 while the average payment to impersonation clusters rose more than 600%. Nothing about the person was the weakness. Everything about the moment was.

Why Knowing Better Doesn’t Stop the Transfer

Social engineering targets states of mind. Urgency and fear of loss as well as deference to authority and the wish to fix a problem quickly all narrow judgment, and technical knowledge cures none of them. Crypto wallet security that assumes informed users will spot the trap is working from an outdated premise. Someone who knows how real support processes run can even find a well-made fake more convincing.

The case record bears that out. Chainalysis describes a scheme in which callers posing as Coinbase customer support defrauded victims of nearly $16 million; they sounded credible because customer data had been obtained through a bribed insider, a breach that exposed nearly 70,000 customers. In the UK, one holder lost nearly $2.5 million in 2025 to a scheme that local police said exploited “fear” and “panic.”

“AI is changing the economics of fraud,” says Jimmy Su, Chief Security Officer at Binance. “Attackers can now create convincing scams faster, cheaper, and at a scale that simply wasn’t possible before. That means security can’t start when a user is about to click ‘confirm.’ By then, we’re already too late.” 

Cheaper production means a sophisticated target now meets a lure built specifically for them. Any defense that depends on the target noticing the deception has to assume it will sometimes fail.

The national numbers show the scale. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center recorded $7.2 billion in crypto investment fraud losses across 61,559 complaints in 2025, and Americans over 60 reported $4.4 billion in crypto-related losses.

The Attack Families Running at Scale

Three families dominate here. The first one is the impersonation of exchanges and officials as well as executives. And then come romance-investment hybrids that groom a target for weeks before introducing a fake trading platform. Finally, fake-support takeovers fall into the third category here, attackers talk users into moving funds to a “secure” wallet.

Chainalysis reports that scam operations buy face-swap software and deepfake tools and large language models from vendors and that the categories increasingly blend into one another. Modular tooling also lets technically unsophisticated groups run campaigns that once required specialist skills.

Hardware doesn’t settle the matter either. Hacken’s first-quarter 2026 data attributed $306 million in losses to phishing and social engineering, including a single $282 million hardware-wallet scam in January. Keeping keys offline didn’t help once the holder was persuaded to act.

Lior Aizik, co-founder and Chief Operating Officer at XBO, has been impersonated by name himself. “These attacks rely on urgency and trust, not technology,” he told CoinDesk. Fewer attempts with larger payoffs is what targeting looks like once deception becomes cheap to personalize. And the phishing data reflects it. CertiK counted 63 phishing incidents in the first half of 2026 down 52.3% YoY. But despite that, losses fell only 10.8% to $366.3 million and four incidents accounted for about 85% of the total.

Where Automated Controls Catch What Persuasion Wins

A scam can win the conversation but the persuaded user still has to move funds through a wallet. The transfer passes through screening, the destination contract through simulation and the approval request through analysis, and none of those checkpoints depend on the user’s state of mind.

“We have to disrupt the attack earlier,” Su says, listing the sequence: “filter the malicious transfer, identify the dangerous address or contract, simulate the transaction, and surface risky approvals before they become losses.” 

Binance reports its Wallet Security Center identified around 4.93 million high-risk transactions across 19 chains in the first half of 2026. Some were blocked automatically; others were abandoned after users saw a risk alert. 

The company doesn’t break out how many followed a social engineering contact, so the data can’t answer that. What it does show is that an alert gives a persuaded user a second chance to stop, while an automatic block doesn’t need one.

Binance’s own post acknowledges that no security tool can protect a decision a user insists on making, which is why these controls work as a backstop. Over the same six months, Binance’s wallet systems also flagged around 996,000 malicious approvals, the kind of standing permission attackers use to drain a wallet after the conversation ends.

Verify Out of Band, Every Time

Human skepticism remains necessary, and on its own it’s no longer enough. Platform controls act as the seatbelt for the moment persuasion wins, and one user habit still matters on top of them. 

Before acting on any request to move funds or change a wallet address, verify it independently through an official channel you already trust. Don’t use contact details or links supplied by the person making the request. Urgency calls for more scrutiny, and a well-built AI scam will always supply plenty of it.
